name: Mini-Games
description: Build complete game engines from scratch. Start with helper functions that teach core game-programming concepts, then implement full games like Tic-Tac-Toe, Hangman, Minesweeper, and Chess.
attribution: Original game logic exercises designed for CodeForge

exercises.title: Shuffle Array
exercises.description: Implement the Fisher-Yates shuffle algorithm to randomly reorder an array in place.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `shuffleArray` that takes an array and returns a new array with the same elements in a random order. The function should not modify the original array.

The Fisher-Yates algorithm works by iterating from the last element to the first, swapping each element with a randomly chosen element that comes before it (or itself).

Example:
```
shuffleArray([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
// Returns: [3, 1, 5, 2, 4] (order varies)
```

The returned array must contain exactly the same elements as the input — no duplicates, no missing values.
hints: The Fisher-Yates algorithm iterates backward through the array. On each step, pick a random index from 0 to the current position and swap those two elements.
Make a copy of the input array first with spread syntax. Loop from the last index down to 1, using `Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1))` to pick the swap target.

exercises.title: Create Card Deck
exercises.description: Generate a standard 52-card playing card deck as an array of card objects.
hints: You need two arrays — one for the four suits and one for the thirteen ranks. Use nested loops to create every combination.
Inside the inner loop, determine the value using conditionals: aces are 11, face cards (J, Q, K) are 10, and number cards use their numeric rank.

exercises.title: Roll Dice
exercises.description: Simulate rolling multiple dice and return the individual rolls along with their sum.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `rollDice` that takes two parameters:
- `count`: the number of dice to roll (default: 1)
- `sides`: the number of sides per die (default: 6)

Return an object with:
- `rolls`: an array of individual roll results (each between 1 and `sides` inclusive)
- `total`: the sum of all rolls

Example:
```
rollDice(3, 6)
// Returns: { rolls: [4, 2, 6], total: 12 } (values vary)

rollDice()
// Returns: { rolls: [3], total: 3 } (single d6)
```
hints: Use `Math.floor(Math.random() * sides) + 1` to generate a single roll between 1 and the number of sides. Loop `count` times to fill the rolls array.
Handle default parameter values at the start of the function. After building the rolls array, use `reduce()` to compute the sum for the total property.

exercises.title: Check Grid Winner
exercises.description: Check a tic-tac-toe board for a winner by scanning rows, columns, and diagonals.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `checkWinner` that takes a 3x3 grid (array of 3 arrays, each with 3 values) and returns the winner.

Each cell contains `"X"`, `"O"`, or `null` (empty). A player wins by filling an entire row, column, or diagonal.

Return:
- `"X"` if X has three in a row
- `"O"` if O has three in a row
- `null` if no winner

Example:
```
checkWinner([
  ["X", "X", "X"],
  ["O", "O", null],
  [null, null, null]
])
// Returns: "X" (top row)
```
hints: There are eight possible winning lines on a 3x3 grid: three rows, three columns, and two diagonals. Check each one separately.

For rows, loop through each row and compare all three cells. For columns, compare cells at the same index across all three rows. For diagonals, check the two fixed diagonal paths. Only return a winner if all three cells match and are not null.

exercises.title: Score Card Hand
exercises.description: Calculate the score of a Blackjack hand, adjusting aces from 11 to 1 to avoid busting.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `scoreHand` that takes an array of card objects (each with a `value` property) and returns the best Blackjack score.

Rules:
- Sum all card values
- If the total exceeds 21 and there are aces (value 11), convert aces to 1 (subtract 10) one at a time until the total is 21 or under, or all aces are converted

Return an object with:
- `total`: the final score
- `soft`: `true` if the hand contains an unconverted ace (still worth 11), `false` otherwise

Example:
```
scoreHand([{ value: 11 }, { value: 5 }])
// Returns: { total: 16, soft: true }

scoreHand([{ value: 11 }, { value: 7 }, { value: 8 }])
// Returns: { total: 16, soft: false } (ace converted to 1)
```
hints: First pass: sum all values and count how many aces are in the hand. Second pass: while the total is over 21 and you still have uncoverted aces, subtract 10 from the total and decrement the ace count.
The hand is "soft" if there is still at least one ace counting as 11 after all adjustments. Track aces with a counter that decreases each time you convert one.

exercises.title: Score Wordle Guess
exercises.description: Score a 5-letter Wordle guess against the target word, returning green, yellow, or gray for each letter.
hints: This requires two passes. First, scan for exact position matches (green) and mark those target positions as used. Second, scan remaining letters for wrong-position matches (yellow), again marking target positions as consumed.

Use a boolean array to track which target positions have been claimed. Green matches get priority in the first pass. In the second pass, skip positions already marked green and only match against unused target positions.

exercises.title: Slide and Merge Row
exercises.description: Implement the core 2048 row mechanic: slide non-zero values left and merge adjacent equal values.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `slideAndMerge` that takes an array of 4 numbers (representing a row in 2048) and returns an object with:
- `row`: the new row after sliding left and merging
- `score`: points earned from merges (sum of all merged tile values)

Rules:
1. Slide all non-zero values to the left (remove gaps)
2. If two adjacent values are equal, merge them into one tile worth double
3. A merged tile cannot merge again in the same move
4. Fill remaining spaces with 0

Example:
```
slideAndMerge([2, 0, 2, 0])
// Returns: { row: [4, 0, 0, 0], score: 4 }

slideAndMerge([2, 2, 2, 2])
// Returns: { row: [4, 4, 0, 0], score: 8 }
```
hints: Start by filtering out all zeros to get just the non-zero values pushed left. Then walk through the compacted array looking for adjacent pairs that match — when found, combine them and skip the second value.

After merging, pad the result array with zeros until it has 4 elements. Track points earned by accumulating the value of each merged tile. Remember that a merged tile cannot merge again in the same move.

exercises.title: Count Grid Neighbors
exercises.description: Count how many of a cell's 8 neighbors in a 2D grid contain a specific value.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function called `countNeighbors` that takes three parameters:
- `grid`: a 2D array (array of arrays)
- `row`: the row index of the target cell
- `col`: the column index of the target cell

Return the count of how many of the cell's 8 surrounding neighbors (up, down, left, right, and 4 diagonals) contain a truthy value.

Edge and corner cells have fewer than 8 neighbors — only count positions that exist within the grid boundaries.

Example:
```
const grid = [
  [1, 0, 0],
  [0, 0, 1],
  [1, 0, 0]
];
countNeighbors(grid, 1, 1)
// Returns: 3 (top-left 1, right 1, bottom-left 1)
```
hints: Use two nested loops with offsets from -1 to +1 for both row and column. This gives you all 9 positions in the 3x3 neighborhood — skip the center (0, 0) offset since that is the cell itself.

Before accessing a neighbor, check that the computed row and column are within the grid boundaries (not negative and not past the last index). Only increment the count for in-bounds positions with truthy values.

exercises.title: Tic-Tac-Toe Engine
exercises.description: Build a complete Tic-Tac-Toe game engine with move validation, turn tracking, and winner detection.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createTicTacToe()` that returns a game object with methods:

- `makeMove(row, col)`: Place the current player's mark on the board. Returns an object `{ valid, winner, draw }`.
  - `valid`: `true` if the move was placed, `false` if the cell is occupied, the game is already over, or the coordinates are out of bounds (row/col must be 0-2)
  - `winner`: `"X"` or `"O"` if the move caused a win, otherwise `null`
  - `draw`: `true` if the board is full with no winner after this move, otherwise `false`
  - On an invalid move, return `{ valid: false, winner: null, draw: false }`
- `getBoard()`: Returns the 3x3 grid as an array of 3 arrays. Empty cells are `null`, filled cells are `"X"` or `"O"`.
- `getCurrentPlayer()`: Returns `"X"` or `"O"` indicating whose turn it is.
- `reset()`: Clears the board to all `null` and sets the current player back to `"X"`.

X always goes first. Turns alternate after each valid move. Once the game ends (win or draw), no further moves are accepted until `reset()` is called.
hints: Use a closure to hold the board state (a 3x3 array of nulls), the current player, and a game-over flag. The `makeMove` method should validate bounds and occupancy before placing a mark.
Write a helper that checks all 8 winning lines (3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals). After placing a mark, check for a winner, then check if the board is full for a draw, then toggle the current player.

exercises.title: Hangman Engine
exercises.description: Build a Hangman game engine that tracks guesses, reveals letters, and counts remaining lives.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createHangman(word, maxLives)` where `word` is the secret word (string) and `maxLives` is the number of wrong guesses allowed (default 6). Returns a game object with:

- `guess(letter)`: Process a single-letter guess (case insensitive). Returns an object `{ valid, correct, alreadyGuessed, gameOver, won }`.
  - `valid`: `false` if the input is not exactly one letter or the game is already over; `true` otherwise
  - `correct`: `true` if the letter is in the word, `false` if not (only meaningful when `valid` is `true`)
  - `alreadyGuessed`: `true` if this letter was already guessed before
  - `gameOver`: `true` if the game ended on this guess
  - `won`: `true` if the player won (all letters revealed), `false` otherwise
  - On an invalid guess, return `{ valid: false, correct: false, alreadyGuessed: false, gameOver: false, won: false }`
- `getDisplay()`: Returns the word as a string where unguessed letters are replaced with underscores (e.g., `"h_llo"`). No spaces between characters.
- `getState()`: Returns `{ guessedLetters, livesRemaining, gameOver, won }` where `guessedLetters` is a sorted array of all guessed letters (lowercase).

All letter matching is case insensitive. The word is stored and displayed in lowercase.
hints: Use a closure with a Set for guessed letters, a lives counter, and game-over/won flags. Convert everything to lowercase at the start. The `guess` method validates input, checks membership, and updates state accordingly.

For `getDisplay`, split the word into characters and map each one: if it is in the guessed set, show the letter; otherwise show an underscore. Join without spaces. Check for a win by testing if every character in the word is in the guessed set.

exercises.title: Memory Match Engine
exercises.description: Build a Memory Match card game engine with pair matching and scoring.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createMemoryGame(pairs, shuffled)` where `pairs` is an array of values (e.g., `["A", "B", "C"]`) and `shuffled` is an optional pre-arranged board array.

If `shuffled` is provided, use it as the card layout directly. If not provided, create the board by doubling the pairs array and shuffling with Fisher-Yates.

Returns a game object:

- `flip(index)`: Flip a card at the given index. Returns `{ valid, value, matched, turnComplete }`.
  - `valid`: `false` if index is out of bounds, the card is already matched, or the card is currently flipped face-up. `true` otherwise.
  - `value`: the card's value if valid, `null` if invalid
  - `matched`: `true` if this was the second flip and the two cards match, `false` otherwise
  - `turnComplete`: `true` after the second flip of a turn, `false` on the first flip
  - After a completed non-matching turn, the next `flip` call should first flip those two cards back face-down, then process the new flip.
- `getBoard()`: Returns an array of objects `{ flipped, matched, value }`. The `value` property is the card's value if `flipped` or `matched` is `true`, otherwise `null`.
- `getScore()`: Returns `{ matches, attempts }` where `matches` is the number of pairs found and `attempts` is the number of completed turns.
- `isComplete()`: Returns `true` when all pairs have been matched.

Each turn consists of flipping two cards. If they match, both stay revealed.
hints: Use a closure with an array of card objects (each having `value`, `flipped`, `matched`). Track the index of the first flipped card and use `null` to know whether you are on the first or second flip of a turn.

When a non-matching turn completes, do not immediately flip the cards back. Instead, on the next `flip` call, check if there is a pending non-matched pair and reset them before processing the new flip. This simulates the brief reveal before cards flip back.

exercises.title: Snake Engine
exercises.description: Build a Snake game engine with grid movement, food spawning, and collision detection.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createSnake(width, height)` that creates a Snake game on a grid of the given dimensions. Returns a game object:

- `move(direction)`: Move the snake one step in the given direction (`"up"`, `"down"`, `"left"`, `"right"`). Returns `{ valid, ate, gameOver, score }`.
  - `valid`: `true` if the move was processed, `false` if the game is already over or direction is invalid
  - `ate`: `true` if the snake ate food on this move
  - `gameOver`: `true` if the snake hit a wall or itself
  - `score`: current score (number of food items eaten)
  - Movement: `"up"` decreases row, `"down"` increases row, `"left"` decreases col, `"right"` increases col
  - When the snake eats food, it grows by one segment (the tail does not move that turn)
  - Wall collision: new head position is outside the grid bounds
  - Self collision: new head position overlaps any existing body segment
- `getState()`: Returns `{ snake, food, score, gameOver }` where `snake` is an array of `{row, col}` objects (head first) and `food` is `{row, col}` or `null` if no food is placed.
- `placeFood(row, col)`: Manually place food at a specific position. Use this for deterministic testing.

The snake starts at the center of the grid (use `Math.floor(width / 2)` for col and `Math.floor(height / 2)` for row), length 1, with no food on the board and score 0.
hints: Use a closure holding the snake as an array of `{row, col}` segments (head at index 0), food position, score, and game-over flag. A direction map converts direction strings to row/col deltas. Compute the new head position and check bounds and self-collision before moving.

To move: unshift the new head onto the snake array. If the snake ate food, increment score and leave the tail in place (the snake grows). Otherwise, pop the tail to maintain the same length. Use `placeFood` to set food position for deterministic testing.

exercises.title: Wordle Engine
exercises.description: Build a complete Wordle game engine with guess validation, letter scoring, and game state management.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createWordle(targetWord)` that takes a 5-letter target word and returns a game object with three methods:

**`guess(word)`** — Submit a 5-letter guess. Returns an object:
- `valid`: boolean indicating if the guess was accepted
- `result`: array of 5 objects, each with `letter` (the guessed letter) and `status` ("green", "yellow", or "gray")
- `gameOver`: boolean
- `won`: boolean

A guess is invalid (valid: false) if:
- The word is not exactly 5 letters
- The game is already over
- The player has already used all 6 guesses

Scoring uses a two-pass algorithm:
1. First pass: mark exact position matches as "green" and consume those target letters
2. Second pass: for remaining letters, mark as "yellow" if the letter exists in unconsumed target positions, otherwise "gray"

This means green takes priority over yellow when handling duplicate letters.

**`getHistory()`** — Returns an array of past guesses. Each entry is an array of `{ letter, status }` objects (the `result` from that guess).

**`getState()`** — Returns `{ guessesRemaining, gameOver, won }`.

Example:
```
const game = createWordle("crane");
game.guess("hello");
// { valid: true, result: [{letter:"h",status:"gray"}, ...], gameOver: false, won: false }
game.guess("crane");
// { valid: true, result: all green, gameOver: true, won: true }
```
hints: Use a closure to track an array of past guesses, a gameOver flag, and a won flag. The guess method should validate input before scoring. Scoring uses two passes: first mark greens, then scan for yellows among unused target letters.

For duplicate letter handling, maintain a `used` boolean array for target positions. Green matches consume a target position in the first pass. In the second pass, yellow matches consume the first available unused target position for that letter.

exercises.title: Blackjack Engine
exercises.description: Build a Blackjack game engine with dealing, hitting, standing, and dealer AI.
hints: Use a closure to track a deck index, player and dealer hand arrays, gameOver, and result. Write a helper `scoreHand` that sums card values and adjusts aces (value 11) down to 1 when the total exceeds 21.

The `stand` method should loop `while (scoreHand(dealerHand) < 17)` drawing cards. After the dealer stops, compare scores: dealer bust or player higher means player wins, dealer higher means dealer wins, equal means push.

exercises.title: Connect Four Engine
exercises.description: Build a Connect Four game engine with gravity-based piece dropping and four-in-a-row detection.
exercises.instructions:
Write a function `createConnectFour()` that creates a 6-row by 7-column Connect Four game. Returns a game object with four methods:

**`dropPiece(col)`** — Drop the current player's piece into the specified column (0-6). Returns:
```
{ valid: boolean, row: number | null, winner: null | "R" | "Y", draw: boolean }
```
- Invalid if the column is out of range (not 0-6), the column is full, or there is already a winner
- The piece falls to the lowest empty row in the column (gravity)
- After placing, check for a winner (4 in a row horizontally, vertically, or diagonally)
- Draw if the board is completely full with no winner

**`getBoard()`** — Returns the 6x7 grid as an array of 6 arrays of 7 values. Each value is `"R"` (red), `"Y"` (yellow), or `null` (empty). Row 0 is the top row.

**`getCurrentPlayer()`** — Returns `"R"` or `"Y"`. Red always goes first.

**`reset()`** — Clears the board, resets to Red's turn, clears any winner.

Example:
```
const game = createConnectFour();
game.dropPiece(3); // Red drops in column 3, falls to row 5
game.dropPiece(3); // Yellow drops in column 3, falls to row 4
game.getCurrentPlayer(); // "R" (Red's turn again)
```
hints: Use a 2D array (6 rows, 7 columns) initialized to null. For `dropPiece`, scan the column from bottom (row 5) to top (row 0) to find the first empty cell. After placing, check all four directions (horizontal, vertical, both diagonals) from the placed position for 4 in a row.

For win detection, check each of the four line directions. For each direction, try all 4 possible starting offsets that could include the placed piece in a run of 4. Toggle `currentPlayer` between 'R' and 'Y' after each valid non-winning move.
